127.title: Confirmation
127.hook: the bishop anoints the forehead with perfumed oil: be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit
127.howItsDone: In the Latin Church most Catholics are confirmed as young people by the bishop, who anoints their foreheads with chrism; Eastern Catholics and the Orthodox receive chrismation as babies right after baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism: water three times, in three names. Your line was your first birthday. Did you find the date, or who was there? Day one hundred twenty-seven.

If you've ever been to a Catholic confirmation, you might remember the smell before anything else. The church is full, teenagers in their best clothes lined up in the aisle, families craning to see. One by one they step up to the bishop, often with a sponsor's hand on their shoulder. The bishop dips his thumb in oil and traces a cross on each forehead. And as he gets closer, the whole front of the church smells faintly sweet, like a perfume counter. That smell has a name. Today's word: chrism.
screen: `TEENAGERS IN THE AISLE.` → `A THUMB, A CROSS, A FOREHEAD.` → `THE SMELL OF PERFUME.`

segments.voice: Chrism is olive oil mixed with balsam, a fragrant resin. Once a year, usually in Holy Week, each bishop consecrates it at a special Mass, and it's sent out to every parish. The word comes from the Greek chrisma, an anointing. And it's the same root as Christ, Christos, which means the anointed one. So to be anointed with chrism is, in a sense, to be made like Christ. In the Bible, kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil to mark them for a task. Confirmation borrows that picture. Where does it come from? In the book of Acts, the people of Samaria hear the Gospel and are baptized. The apostles in Jerusalem send Peter and John, and in the Douay-Rheims, "they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Confirmation, Catholics say, continues that moment. As the bishop anoints, he says, in the English form, be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit. Sealed, like wax pressed with a signet ring: a mark that says this belongs to someone. The Catholic Church teaches confirmation completes baptism and strengthens a person to live the faith in public. Tradition names seven gifts of the Spirit, drawn from Isaiah: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord. The timing differs. In Eastern churches, including Eastern Catholics and the Orthodox, the priest anoints babies right after baptism; they call it chrismation. In the Latin Church, it's usually given years later, or to adults at Easter. Many choose a saint's name to take with them.
screen: `OLIVE OIL AND BALSAM.` · `CHRISMA: THE SAME ROOT AS CHRIST.` · `HANDS LAID ON IN SAMARIA.` · `SEVEN GIFTS OF THE SPIRIT.` · then, large: `SEALED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for one gift. Settle, and breathe. Listen to the seven again, slowly: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord. Fortitude is courage that lasts. Counsel is knowing what to do. Piety is a warm love for God. Which one do you need this week? Pick one. If you pray, you can ask the Holy Spirit for it by name. If you don't, just hold it as a hope, the thing you'd want to be marked with. The bell holds the time.
Chrism. Olive oil and balsam, blessed by the bishop, from the same Greek root as Christ. The oil of confirmation. Today's word.
Your line: sealed. Today, when you need your one gift, touch your forehead for a second and remember you're marked, not alone. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

options: baptize them all again, properly.

fork.reveal: Peter and John go down, and "they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Catholics see confirmation in that moment.

what it means: a sacrament that completes baptism, sealing a person with the Holy Spirit through chrism and the bishop's hand.

128.title: The Eucharist
128.hook: the source and summit of the Christian life (CCC 1324)
128.howItsDone: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, at least on Sundays for many, usually after a first Communion around age seven, and fast for an hour beforehand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chrism, the sweet oil of confirmation. Your line was sealed. Which gift of the Spirit did you ask for? Day one hundred twenty-eight.

Think of a river you know. Follow it back far enough and it starts somewhere small: a spring in the hills, water coming up out of the ground. Follow it the other way and it ends in the sea, where all its water was headed all along. The source and the sea. Now think of a mountain. You start at the bottom, and every path you take is really about one thing: getting to the top. The Catholic Church uses two pictures like these, source and summit, for one sacrament. Today, the Eucharist.
screen: `A SPRING IN THE HILLS.` → `A PATH TO THE TOP.` → `SOURCE AND SUMMIT.`

segments.voice: Eucharist is a Greek word, eucharistia, and it means thanksgiving. At the Last Supper, the Gospels say, Jesus took bread and gave thanks. In the Douay-Rheims, Luke has him say: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." From the very beginning, Christians did. Around the year 150, a writer named Justin Martyr described Christians meeting on Sunday, reading the apostles and prophets, and sharing bread and wine over which thanks had been given. That shape is still the Mass. We've already walked through the Mass piece by piece, and the consecration. Today's idea is bigger: where the Eucharist sits in everything else. The Second Vatican Council called it the source and summit of the whole Christian life, and the Catechism repeats it in paragraph 1324. Source: the other sacraments, the Church's work, a Catholic's prayer, all flow out of it, like a river from its spring. Summit: they all lead back to it, like paths up a mountain. Baptism brings you to the table. Confirmation strengthens you to live what you receive there. Confession clears the way back to it. Priests are ordained above all to celebrate it. Catholics believe that in the Eucharist Jesus himself is truly present, body and blood, soul and divinity, which is why they call it the sacrament of sacraments. Christians understand the table in different ways. The Orthodox also believe in a real change. Lutherans speak of a real presence in their own terms. Many other Protestants receive the Lord's Supper as a memorial. All of them keep the table.
screen: `EUCHARISTIA: THANKSGIVING.` · `SUNDAY BREAD, SINCE JUSTIN, C. 150.` · `SOURCE: EVERYTHING FLOWS FROM IT.` · `SUMMIT: EVERYTHING LEADS TO IT.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BODY, WHICH IS GIVEN FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with two words, source and summit. Settle, and breathe. On the in-breath, think source: what is the spring your day comes out of? Rest, love, a person, God. On the out-breath, think summit: what is your day really climbing toward? Don't answer quickly. Just let the two words go back and forth with your breathing. If you pray, you can give thanks, which is what the word Eucharist means. The bell holds the time.
The Eucharist. From the Greek for thanksgiving. For Catholics, the source that everything flows from, and the summit everything climbs toward. Today's word.
Your line: everything flows from the table. Today, at one meal, pause before you eat and give thanks, even silently, even for ten seconds. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

129.title: Reconciliation
129.hook: the sacrament of return, where sins are forgiven through a priest (CCC 1422)
129.howItsDone: Catholics go to confession by speaking their sins to a priest, in a confessional or face to face, and receive absolution; many parishes offer it on Saturday afternoons and especially in Advent and Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Eucharist, source and summit. Your line was everything flows from the table. Did you pause and give thanks at a meal? Day one hundred twenty-nine.

There's a story Jesus tells about a son who takes his inheritance early, leaves home, and spends it all. He ends up feeding pigs and wishing he could eat what they eat. So he rehearses a speech, and starts the long walk home. And the father, in the Douay-Rheims, "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." He doesn't even let the son finish the speech. Catholics say there's a sacrament built on that run. Today: reconciliation.
screen: `A SON WHO SPENT IT ALL.` → `THE LONG WALK HOME.` → `THE FATHER RUNS.`

segments.voice: This sacrament has several names, and each one shows a side of it. Confession, because you say out loud what you've done. Penance, because you turn around and begin to make amends. And reconciliation, because the point is being brought back together. The Latin reconciliare means to make friends again, to bring back into council. Catholics believe it's the ordinary way God forgives sins committed after baptism. Where does it come from? In John's Gospel, on the evening of the resurrection, Jesus breathes on the apostles. In the Douay-Rheims: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them: and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained." The Catholic Church reads that as Jesus handing on the power to forgive, which is why a priest hears confession. A natural question is: why tell a person? Why not just tell God? Catholics answer in a few ways. Sin isn't only private; it hurts a whole body of people, so the return has a human face too. Saying it aloud makes it real, and hearing the words of forgiveness aloud makes that real as well. And the priest, they believe, acts in the person of Christ, so it's God who forgives. Catholics are asked to go at least once a year if they've committed a serious sin, and many go far more often. Other Christians do this differently: the Orthodox also have confession to a priest; Anglicans offer it but don't require it; most Protestants confess to God directly and to one another. Tomorrow's sacrament heals too, in a different way.
screen: `CONFESSION, PENANCE, RECONCILIATION.` · `RECONCILIARE: TO MAKE FRIENDS AGAIN.` · `WHOSE SINS YOU SHALL FORGIVE.` · `WHY SAY IT TO A PERSON?` · then, large: `THE FATHER RUNS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of what you'd want forgiven. Settle, and breathe. No need to list everything. Just let one thing come up: something you said, or didn't do, that still sits in you. Don't argue with it and don't punish yourself. Just look at it. Then picture the son on the road, and the father running before the speech is even finished. If you pray, you can hand that one thing to God. If you don't, just imagine being met halfway. The bell holds the time.
Reconciliation. From the Latin for making friends again. The sacrament of return, where Catholics confess to a priest and hear that they're forgiven. Today's word.
Your line: there's always a way back. Today, take one small step toward someone you're at odds with. A message, a smile, a hello. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

130.title: Anointing of the sick
130.hook: not only for the dying; oil for anyone seriously ill or old (CCC 1514)
130.howItsDone: A Catholic who is seriously ill, frail with age or facing major surgery can ask a priest for the anointing, at home, in hospital, or at a parish Mass for the sick; it can be received more than once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reconciliation, the sacrament of return. Your line was there's always a way back. Did you take one small step toward someone? Day one hundred thirty.

A hospital room, late afternoon. A woman in her seventies is going in for heart surgery tomorrow. Her daughter has called the parish, and a priest comes in with a small oil stock in his pocket, the size of a lipstick. The daughter looks nervous. Isn't this, she whispers, what they do when someone's dying? The priest smiles. It's a common mix-up. Her mother isn't dying. She's sick, and scared, and that's exactly who this is for. Today, the anointing of the sick.
screen: `A HOSPITAL ROOM, THE DAY BEFORE.` → `ISN'T THIS FOR THE DYING?` → `IT'S FOR THE SICK.`

segments.voice: For centuries this sacrament was called extreme unction, which means the last anointing, and in practice it was often saved for the very end. So many people still think of it that way: the priest arrives, and it's time to say goodbye. After the Second Vatican Council, the Church changed the name and the emphasis. It's the anointing of the sick, and the Catechism says it's for anyone who begins to be in danger because of serious illness or old age. Before major surgery. When a chronic illness gets worse. When age makes a person frail. And it can be received again, if the illness returns or worsens. The roots are in the letter of James. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." James goes on to say the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. The priest lays his hands on the person's head in silence, then anoints the forehead and the hands with the oil of the sick, which the bishop blesses once a year. Only a priest can give it. What do Catholics believe it does? Strength, peace and courage to face the illness, union with Christ's own suffering, forgiveness, and sometimes, if God wills, bodily healing. It doesn't replace doctors. Catholics go to both. When someone is truly near death, the priest may also hear their confession and give Communion, called viaticum, food for the journey. Those together are what people mean by last rites.
screen: `NOT ONLY THE LAST ANOINTING.` · `IS ANY MAN SICK AMONG YOU?` · `HANDS, OIL, FOREHEAD AND PALMS.` · `STRENGTH, PEACE, AND SOMETIMES HEALING.` · then, large: `THE SICK ARE NOT FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who is ill. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is sick or in the hospital, or very old and frail. See their face. Picture the room they're in. If you know what they're afraid of, hold that too. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, or say James's words to yourself: is any man sick among you. If you don't pray, simply keep them company in your mind for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Anointing of the sick. Oil on the forehead and hands, for anyone seriously ill or old, not only the dying. Today's word.
Your line: the sick are not forgotten. Today, send one message, or make one call, to someone who is ill. Ask how they are, and then listen. Day one hundred thirty.

131.title: Holy orders
131.hook: deacons, priests and bishops ordained by the laying on of hands
131.howItsDone: Catholic deacons, priests and bishops are ordained by a bishop, usually in a cathedral, through the silent laying on of hands and a prayer of consecration, after years of formation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the anointing of the sick. Your line was the sick are not forgotten. Who did you call or keep in mind? Day one hundred thirty-one.

At one point in an ordination Mass, a young man in a white robe walks to the front of a packed cathedral and lies down. Flat on the floor, face down, arms at his sides. The whole congregation kneels and sings a long list of saints' names, asking each one to pray for him. It goes on for minutes. His mother is usually in tears. It's one of the most startling things you'll see in a Catholic church: a person giving his whole body to the ground before he's given a job. Today's word: ordination.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN LIES FACE DOWN.` → `A LONG LIST OF SAINTS.` → `HIS WHOLE BODY TO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Ordination comes from the Latin ordo, an order or rank, the word Romans used for the groups that made up their society. The sacrament is called holy orders, plural, because there are three: deacons, priests and bishops. The names are Greek. Deacon is diakonos, a servant, someone who waits on tables. Priest comes, through old English, from presbyteros, an elder. And bishop comes from episkopos, an overseer. Each one is a kind of serving. The sign is very old: hands laid on the head in silence. In the book of Acts, the first seven deacons are chosen to care for widows, and in the Douay-Rheims, "they praying, imposed hands upon them." Paul later reminds Timothy of the gift that came to him through the laying on of hands. At an ordination today, the bishop lays his hands on the candidate's head without a word, then prays the prayer of consecration. At a priest's ordination, every priest present comes up and lays on hands too. Catholics believe this sacrament, like baptism, marks a person for good. Priests celebrate the Eucharist and hear confessions; deacons baptize, preach, witness marriages and serve the poor; bishops lead a diocese and ordain others. In the Latin Church, priests and bishops are normally celibate, while permanent deacons can be married, and Eastern Catholic churches have married priests. The Church ordains only men, and teaches it has no authority to do otherwise; some Catholics hope that will change. Other Christians understand ministry differently: the Orthodox keep the same three orders, while most Protestant churches ordain ministers but don't count ordination as a sacrament.
screen: `ORDO: AN ORDER, A RANK.` · `SERVANT, ELDER, OVERSEER.` · `HANDS LAID ON IN SILENCE.` · `MARKED FOR GOOD, TO SERVE.` · then, large: `CALLED TO SERVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a priest, deacon or minister you've known. Settle, and breathe. Maybe the one who baptized you, or buried your grandmother, or just said something kind after a service. If you don't know one, think of anyone whose job is to look after others: a nurse, a teacher, a coach. See their face. Think about how tired they might be. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Ordination. From the Latin for an order. Deacons, priests and bishops, made by the laying on of hands to serve. Today's word.
Your line: called to serve. Today, thank one person who serves you, a priest, a pastor, a nurse, a bus driver, out loud and by name. Day one hundred thirty-one.

132.title: Matrimony
132.hook: in the Latin Church the couple are the ministers; they give the sacrament to each other
132.howItsDone: Catholics usually marry at a Mass or wedding service in church, exchanging vows before a priest or deacon and two witnesses, after a period of marriage preparation with the parish.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ordination: deacons, priests and bishops, and hands laid on in silence. Your line was called to serve. Who did you thank by name? Day one hundred thirty-two.

Here's a trivia question that surprises most Catholics. At a Catholic wedding, who gives the sacrament? Most people would say the priest. He's the one in vestments, standing in the middle, asking the questions. But in the Latin Church, the answer is: the bride and the groom. The priest or deacon is there as the Church's witness. The two people holding hands are the ones doing it. They give the sacrament to each other. Today, the last of the seven sacraments: matrimony.
screen: `WHO GIVES THE SACRAMENT?` → `NOT THE PRIEST.` → `THE BRIDE AND THE GROOM.`

segments.voice: Matrimony comes from Latin, matrimonium, built on mater, mother. It's an old Roman word, looking ahead to family. In the Latin Church, the heart of the sacrament is consent: two people freely saying yes to each other, for life, in front of witnesses. That's why the couple are the ministers. Their promise is the sign. The priest or deacon asks, and blesses, and receives the vows for the Church. In the Eastern churches it's understood differently: the priest's blessing is essential, and the couple are crowned, as a king and queen of a new little kingdom. Jesus speaks about marriage in Matthew's Gospel, going back to Genesis. In the Douay-Rheims: "Therefore now they are not two, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let no man put asunder." Paul, writing to the Ephesians about husbands and wives, says in the Douay-Rheims, "This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the church." The Latin Bible used the word sacramentum there, and it helped shape how the Church came to see marriage: a human love that shows God's own faithful love. Catholics understand it as lifelong, faithful, and open to children. So the Church doesn't recognize divorce as ending a valid marriage, though it can declare, after careful review, that a marriage was never valid to begin with. Other Christians see marriage in different ways: many Protestant churches treat it as holy but not a sacrament, and the Orthodox, in some cases, allow a second marriage. That completes the seven: three to bring you in, two to heal, two to serve.
screen: `MATRIMONIUM, FROM MATER, MOTHER.` · `THE COUPLE ARE THE MINISTERS.` · `NOT TWO, BUT ONE FLESH.` · `THIS IS A GREAT SACRAMENT.` · then, large: `TWO MINISTERS, ONE PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a married couple. Settle, and breathe. Think of two people you know who have been together a long time. Your grandparents, your parents, neighbors, friends. Picture them on an ordinary day: one making coffee, the other reading out the news. Think of what it's taken them to keep that promise. The bad years, the sick years, the funny ones. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just be glad for them. The bell holds the time.
Matrimony. From the Latin for mother. The sacrament two people give each other, with their own promise. Today's word.

Your line: two ministers, one promise. That's the seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, reconciliation, anointing, orders, matrimony. Today, tell a couple you know what you admire in them. Day one hundred thirty-two.

133.title: The examination of conscience
133.hook: a slow look back using the commandments or the beatitudes
133.howItsDone: Before confession, and often each night, Catholics examine their conscience with a printed guide based on the Ten Commandments, the Beatitudes or the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, matrimony, the sacrament a couple give each other. Your line was two ministers, one promise. Did you tell a couple what you admire? Day one hundred thirty-three.

You know the feeling of lying in bed at night and replaying the day. That thing you said at lunch. The email you sent too fast. Your brain runs the tape, again and again, and it isn't kind about it. Now imagine doing the same review on purpose, slowly, with a guide, and with a different voice: not a prosecutor, more like a good doctor. Honest about what's wrong, and on your side. Catholics have a name for that, and this week we'll follow it all the way into the confessional. Today's word: conscience.
screen: `REPLAYING THE DAY AT NIGHT.` → `NOT A PROSECUTOR.` → `A GOOD DOCTOR.`

segments.voice: Conscience comes from Latin, conscientia: knowing with. Knowing something together with yourself, the part of you that sees what you did and knows what it meant. The Catholic Church teaches that conscience is where a person is alone with God, a kind of inner sanctuary where God's voice can be heard, and that everyone is bound to follow a well-formed conscience. John Henry Newman, the English convert and cardinal, put it memorably in 1875: "Conscience is the aboriginal Vicar of Christ." Aboriginal meaning first, original: before any pope or priest, there's that voice within. An examination of conscience is the practice of listening to it on purpose. Before confession, Catholics often go slowly through a guide. The most common uses the Ten Commandments: have I put anything in God's place? Have I been honest? Have I treated my parents with respect? Another uses the Beatitudes: have I been merciful? Have I made peace, or stirred things up? Some use the works of mercy. Many do a short version every night. Here's the key, and it's in today's carry. An examination is not a trial where you're the defendant. Catholic spiritual writers keep warning against scrupulosity, a harsh, anxious picking at yourself that never finds rest. The point of looking is to see clearly enough to be healed. You look honestly, because you can't ask forgiveness for what you won't admit. And you look without harshness, because the one you're looking with, Catholics believe, is merciful. Tomorrow we walk through the door of the confessional.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a slow look back. Settle, and breathe. Go back through the last day, like a film, from waking up until now. Where were you patient? Where were you short with someone? Where were you honest? Where did you shade the truth? Notice, don't judge. If something stands out, just name it to yourself, plainly. Then name one thing you did well, because that belongs in the look back too. If you pray, you can hand both to God. The bell holds the time.
Conscience. From the Latin for knowing with. The inner voice Catholics believe is where a person meets God, and a slow, honest look back by its light. Today's word.

Your line: look honestly, not harshly. This week: baptism, chrism, the Eucharist, reconciliation, anointing, ordination, matrimony, and conscience. Tonight, before sleep, give the day one gentle look back. Day one hundred thirty-three.
